transactions.description: The owner invests $10,000 cash in the business.
transactions.explanation: Cash is an asset. It goes up, so debit Cash. Owner's Capital is equity. It goes up, so credit Owner's Capital.

transactions.description: The owner invests $5,000 cash and equipment worth $3,000 in the business.
transactions.explanation: Cash and Equipment are assets. Both go up, so debit both. Owner's Capital goes up by the total, $8,000, so credit it. Total debits equal total credits.

transactions.description: The business borrows $20,000 from a bank and signs a note.
transactions.explanation: Cash goes up, so debit Cash. Notes Payable is a liability. It goes up, so credit Notes Payable.

transactions.description: The owner takes $1,200 cash from the business for personal use.
transactions.explanation: Drawings reduce owner's equity. The Drawings account goes up, so debit it. Cash goes down, so credit Cash.

transactions.description: The business pays $5,000 to the bank to repay part of the note (no interest).
transactions.explanation: The liability goes down, so debit Notes Payable. Cash goes down, so credit Cash.

transactions.description: The business buys office supplies for $300 cash.
transactions.explanation: Supplies are an asset. They go up, so debit Supplies. Cash goes down, so credit Cash.

transactions.description: The business buys office supplies for $450 on account (pays later).
transactions.explanation: Supplies go up, so debit Supplies. The business owes the seller. Accounts Payable is a liability and it goes up, so credit it.

transactions.description: The business buys equipment for $6,000 cash.
transactions.explanation: Equipment is an asset and it goes up, so debit Equipment. Cash goes down, so credit Cash.

transactions.description: The business buys equipment for $9,000. It pays $3,000 cash and signs a note for the rest.
transactions.explanation: Equipment goes up by the full cost, so debit $9,000. Cash goes down $3,000, so credit Cash. The rest, $6,000, is a new liability, so credit Notes Payable.

transactions.description: The business buys merchandise for resale for $2,500 on account.
transactions.explanation: Inventory is an asset. It goes up, so debit Inventory. Accounts Payable is a liability. It goes up, so credit it.

transactions.description: The business buys merchandise for resale for $1,800 cash.
transactions.explanation: Inventory goes up, so debit Inventory. Cash goes down, so credit Cash.

transactions.description: The business pays $1,200 cash for a one-year insurance policy that starts today.
transactions.explanation: The business pays for coverage it has not used yet. That is an asset, Prepaid Insurance. Debit it. Cash goes down, so credit Cash.

transactions.description: The business pays $3,000 cash for three months of rent in advance.
transactions.explanation: Rent paid in advance is an asset, Prepaid Rent. Debit it. Cash goes down, so credit Cash.

transactions.description: The business buys land for $30,000 cash.
transactions.explanation: Land is an asset and it goes up, so debit Land. Cash goes down, so credit Cash.

transactions.description: The business performs services for a customer and receives $800 cash.
transactions.explanation: Cash goes up, so debit Cash. Revenue goes up, so credit Service Revenue.

transactions.description: The business performs services for a customer on account for $1,500. The customer will pay later.
transactions.explanation: The business earned the revenue now, so credit Service Revenue. The customer owes the business. Accounts Receivable is an asset and it goes up, so debit it.

transactions.description: A customer pays $1,500 cash for services the business performed last month on account.
transactions.explanation: Cash goes up, so debit Cash. The customer no longer owes the business. Accounts Receivable goes down, so credit it. The revenue was recorded last month.

transactions.description: A customer pays the business $2,400 cash in advance for services the business will perform next month.
transactions.explanation: Cash goes up, so debit Cash. The business has not earned the money yet. It owes the customer services. Unearned Revenue is a liability and it goes up, so credit it.

transactions.description: The business performs $800 of the services that a customer paid for in advance.
transactions.explanation: The liability goes down as the business earns the money, so debit Unearned Revenue. Revenue goes up, so credit Service Revenue.

transactions.description: The business sells merchandise to a customer for $900 cash. Ignore the cost of the goods.
transactions.explanation: Cash goes up, so debit Cash. Revenue goes up, so credit Sales Revenue.

transactions.description: The business sells merchandise on account for $1,200. The merchandise cost $700. Record the sale and the cost of the goods in one entry (perpetual inventory).
transactions.explanation: Part 1: the sale. Accounts Receivable goes up (debit $1,200) and Sales Revenue goes up (credit $1,200). Part 2: the cost. Cost of Goods Sold is an expense and it goes up (debit $700). Inventory goes down (credit $700).

transactions.description: The business receives $120 cash of interest on its savings account.
transactions.explanation: Cash goes up, so debit Cash. Revenue goes up, so credit Interest Revenue.

transactions.description: A tenant pays the business $600 cash of rent for this month.
transactions.explanation: Cash goes up, so debit Cash. Revenue goes up, so credit Rent Revenue.

transactions.description: The business pays $1,000 cash for this month's rent.
transactions.explanation: Expenses go up with a debit, so debit Rent Expense. Cash goes down, so credit Cash.

transactions.description: The business pays $2,000 cash in wages to its employees.
transactions.explanation: Debit the expense, Wages Expense. Credit Cash because cash goes down.

transactions.description: The business pays a $180 cash utility bill for this month.
transactions.explanation: Debit the expense, Utilities Expense. Credit Cash because cash goes down.

transactions.description: The business pays $400 cash for advertising.
transactions.explanation: Debit the expense, Advertising Expense. Credit Cash because cash goes down.

transactions.description: The business receives a $220 utility bill. It will pay the bill later (record it as an account payable).
transactions.explanation: The expense happened now, so debit Utilities Expense. The business owes the money. Accounts Payable goes up, so credit it.

transactions.description: The business pays $450 cash to a supplier for supplies it bought on account last month.
transactions.explanation: The liability goes down, so debit Accounts Payable. Cash goes down, so credit Cash. The supplies were recorded last month.

transactions.description: The business pays $350 cash to repair its equipment.
transactions.explanation: Debit the expense, Repairs Expense. Credit Cash because cash goes down.

transactions.description: At the end of the month, a count shows the business used $200 of its supplies.
transactions.explanation: Used supplies are an expense, so debit Supplies Expense. The asset Supplies goes down, so credit Supplies.

transactions.description: The business paid $1,200 for a 12-month insurance policy. One month has now passed.
transactions.explanation: One month of cost is $1,200 / 12 = $100. Debit Insurance Expense for $100. The asset Prepaid Insurance goes down, so credit it.

transactions.description: The business paid $3,000 for three months of rent in advance. One month has now passed.
transactions.explanation: One month of cost is $3,000 / 3 = $1,000. Debit Rent Expense for $1,000. The asset Prepaid Rent goes down, so credit it.

transactions.description: At the end of the period, the business records $500 of depreciation on its equipment.
transactions.explanation: Debit the expense, Depreciation Expense. Credit Accumulated Depreciation. It is a contra asset account. It reduces the value of Equipment, and a credit increases it.

transactions.description: At the end of the period, employees have earned $1,400 of wages that the business has not paid yet.
transactions.explanation: The expense belongs to this period, so debit Wages Expense. The business owes its employees. Wages Payable is a liability and it goes up, so credit it.

transactions.description: In the next period, the business pays the $1,400 of wages it owed at the end of last period.
transactions.explanation: The liability goes down, so debit Wages Payable. Cash goes down, so credit Cash. The expense was recorded last period.

transactions.description: At the end of the period, $90 of interest has built up on the note payable. The business has not paid it yet.
transactions.explanation: The expense belongs to this period, so debit Interest Expense. The business owes the interest. Interest Payable is a liability and it goes up, so credit it.

transactions.description: At the end of the period, the business has earned $60 of interest on a bank deposit but has not received it yet.
transactions.explanation: The business earned the revenue now, so credit Interest Revenue. The bank owes the business. Interest Receivable is an asset and it goes up, so debit it.

transactions.description: At the end of the period, the business estimates that $350 of its accounts receivable will not be collected (allowance method).
transactions.explanation: Debit the expense, Bad Debt Expense. Credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts. It is a contra asset account. It reduces Accounts Receivable, and a credit increases it.

transactions.description: The business writes off a customer's $200 account as uncollectible (allowance method).
transactions.explanation: The business already set aside an allowance. Debit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts to use it. Credit Accounts Receivable because the customer's balance is removed. No new expense is recorded.
